title: How to Learn Buddhism
author: Zhiyu

inline.s: Return to the Academy
Return to the Garden
In its cultivation there are stages by which one enters;
In its realization there is a true attainment that one reaches on one’s own.
The aim of learning Buddhism is: to seek the Buddha’s Way above, and to transform sentient beings below. This
is also the great mission of every student of the Dharma. How, then, is one to reach this aim and fulfill this mission?

To learn Buddhism, one must first arouse the bodhi mind, for the bodhi mind is the solemn vow of the great mission to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings; it is the lighthouse for crossing the sea of birth-and-death suffering, and the driving force for braving the wind and waves.

Master Chewu said: “If the great mind (the bodhi mind) is not aroused, then outwardly one cannot resonate with the Buddhas, and inwardly one cannot tally with one’s own nature; above, one cannot perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way; below, one cannot broadly benefit the multitudes of beings. How can one be released from love and attachment without beginning? How can one resolve grievances and enmities without beginning? The karmic offenses amassed over kalpas are hard to confess away; the wholesome roots amassed over kalpas are hard to bring to maturity. Whatever one practices, obstacles multiply; even should one achieve something, one ends by falling into the partial and the lesser. Therefore one must arouse the great bodhi mind in accordance with one’s nature.” (The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)

Master Xing’an’s Exhortation to Arouse the Bodhi Mind says: “The essential gate for entering the Way is to put the arousal of the mind first; the urgent task of practice is to give priority to establishing vows. Once the vow is established, sentient beings can be delivered; once the mind is aroused, the Buddha Way can be accomplished. If one does not arouse the vast mind and establish firm vows, then even after passing through numberless kalpas one still remains in the round of rebirth; though one may practice, it is all toil in vain. Hence the Flower Ornament Sūtra says: ‘To forget the bodhi mind and yet cultivate all wholesome dharmas is called the karma of Māra.’ If even forgetting it is so, how much worse never to have aroused it! Thus we know that whoever wishes to learn the vehicle of the Tathāgata must first fully arouse the vows of a bodhisattva; this cannot be delayed.”

Peng Jiqing’s Preface to Master Xing’an’s Posthumous Works says: “In the past, when our World-Honored One had just attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: ‘How wonderful! How wonderful! There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata. It is only because of deluded thought, inversion, and attachment that they cannot realize it. If they part from deluded thought, the all-knowing wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom will manifest before them.’ I have long failed to understand this: why, for all the misery their deluded thought and attachment bring, do these sentient beings not part from them? And why, when it comes to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, do they still shrink from difficulty and not realize it? Yet in the end they flee from their father, drift through long kalpas, and willingly become lowly hired servants, never thinking to turn back? There is no other reason: it is simply that they are not awakened. The bodhi mind is none other than a different name for awakening. The moment one awakens, the deluded thoughts and attachments before one are entirely the wisdom of the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata’s wisdom has no essence of its own, taking the deluded thoughts of sentient beings as its essence; and the deluded thoughts of sentient beings have no essence of their own, taking the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their essence. Just as water forms waves, and every wave is water, from the very beginning they are ultimately to abide in nirvāṇa without remainder. Therefore the difference between the awakened and the unawakened must never be concealed from oneself or befogged. Reflecting on this with sudden astonishment, and with a crack (xū — the sound of skin and bone separating), comprehension dawns; then the arousal of the bodhi mind will naturally be an overwhelming force that none can resist. Once this mind is aroused, the all-knowing wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom manifest before one — what need is there to seek anything elsewhere?”

The Venerable Xuyun said: “Cultivation has no other cultivation; only recognize the head of the road. Once the road’s head is recognized, birth and death both cease.” The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “If the ground-cause is not true, the fruit will come out crooked.” Therefore, for a student of Buddhism to possess right understanding is of the utmost importance. The curriculum of the Practice-as-Taught Online Buddhist Academy (the Academy’s website:
www.cfolu.com

) is designed so that, through systematic study and practice, one establishes right understanding and carries it out in one’s conduct. Its course of study is divided into four stages: 1. Ceasing evil and practicing good; 2. taking the precepts as the foundation; 3. prajñā dispelling delusion; 4. the Land of Ultimate Bliss as the refuge. The goals of cultivation are: to arouse the bodhi mind, to comprehend the ultimate truth, to have faith and vows and recitation of the name, and single-mindedness without confusion; to firmly grasp the fundamental theories of Buddhism, and to acquire the ability to read the original texts of sūtras and treatises directly, thereby laying a solid foundation for propagating the Dharma and benefiting beings. inline.s: Learning Buddhism is a process of turning evil into good, confusion into awakening, and the ordinary into the holy. Therefore the study of sūtras and treatises must ultimately be carried into actual practice (in thought and conduct).

The method of study and practice is: hearing → reflection → cultivation. Hearing is listening to the teaching (including reading it); reflection is pondering its meaning; cultivation is putting its meaning into actual practice. Through this process, we transform our ignorant views into right understanding and right views, and carry them into body (conduct), speech, and mind. In this process, repeated habituation is of the utmost importance; only through ceaseless habituation can one awaken into the Buddha’s understanding, give rise to the wisdom of discernment, and guide one’s own actions.
Generally speaking, when studying a sūtra or treatise, one should first divide it into a number of units, for instance by chapter or section.
First, for each unit:
Coarse reading. Read the unit three times to build an overall sense of it, so that you clearly know what the unit specifically contains.

Close reading. Divide it into paragraphs, write out the main idea of each paragraph and the central theme of the unit, and make sure every difficult character and difficult sentence is clearly understood.

Intensive reading. Through intensive reading, remember the meanings of technical terms, be able to recite the essential phrases and verses from memory, and be able to explain the unit — especially to expound on the difficult points and difficult sentences.
Then:
Master the whole book. The requirement is: write out the central theme and the overall thread of the whole book, and be able to summarize the entire book without looking at the text.

5. Habituation. Through ceaseless habituation, awaken into the Buddha’s understanding, give rise to the wisdom of discernment, and guide your own actions. This step is extremely important; one must constantly apply, test, transform, and elevate oneself amid circumstances.

For beginners, starting directly from the original texts of sūtras and treatises is quite difficult; it is best to begin from annotated editions. Once one has acquired a certain ability, one should read the original texts directly, for in this way the wisdom of discernment arises more readily. Therefore, when studying with annotated editions, one should deliberately cultivate the ability to read the originals directly. inline.s: The Lotus Sūtra says: “The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house. Filled with manifold sufferings, they are greatly to be feared. There are always the sorrows of birth, old age, sickness, and death — such fires blaze on without cease.” Therefore, the Buddha taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, speaking of the sheep cart (the vehicle of the śrāvakas), the deer cart (the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas), the ox cart (the vehicle of the bodhisattvas), and even the great white ox cart (the Buddha vehicle), all in order to rescue sentient beings from this burning house of the three realms.

[Three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by beings who still have the two desires of lust and food, extending from the six desire heavens above, through humans and animals in the middle, down to hungry ghosts and the hells below. The form realm is the world inhabited by beings who have ended the two desires of lust and food but still possess a form body, including the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who no longer have a form body but dwell with their mind-consciousness in profound and subtle meditative absorption, including the four formless heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothing Whatsoever, and the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all states in which ordinary beings undergo the round of birth and death; therefore the Buddhist practitioner first aims to end birth and death by leaving the three realms.

How, then, does one leave the three realms? The answer is: recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss — this is the easiest, quickest, and surest path. And within the methods of Buddha-recitation, recitation of the name is in turn the easiest, quickest, and surest, praised by the ancient masters as “a shortcut within the shortcut (a shortcut among shortcuts).”

All other methods require one to cut off all afflictions in order to leave the three realms, whereas recitation of the name requires only that one be able to suppress afflictions by means of the Buddha’s name
, with single-mindedness without confusion
at the hour of death

one is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Suppressing afflictions by means of the Buddha’s name, compared with cutting off all afflictions, is indeed vastly easier. And once one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one immediately realizes the stage of non-retrogression; under the guidance of Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and with the mutual help and encouragement of the great assembly of pure bodhisattvas, one quickly attains Buddhahood
, fulfilling the bodhi vow
. Therefore, recitation of the name is the most excellent method for ending birth and death.

There are many concrete methods of name-recitation, but their goal is all the same: to achieve single-mindedness without confusion, so as to ensure that at the hour of death Amitābha Buddha comes to welcome one. In the Amitābha Sūtra, the Buddha says: “If virtuous men or virtuous women hear of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast to his name — for one day, for two days, for three days, for four days, for five days, for six days, for seven days — attaining single-mindedness without confusion, then when such a person comes to the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the host of sages, appears before them. At the end of life the person’s mind is not inverted, and they are immediately reborn in Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

The greatest obstacle to single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation is deluded thought. In the book Aware Buddha-Recitation, the causes of deluded thought, and how to overcome it effectively, are analyzed in detail, along with the concrete steps and methods of study and practice for attaining single-mindedness without confusion in Buddha-recitation.
